title: $700,000 Mortgage Payment by Rate & Term (2026)
metaDescription: A $700,000 mortgage costs $4,424.48/mo at 6.5% over 30 years ($6,097.75 on 15). See payments at 5–7.5%, total interest, and the income needed.

hero.lede: Principal-and-interest payments on a $700,000 home loan across 5.0%–7.5% rates and 15/30-year terms, plus total interest, a first-year amortization schedule, and the income the 28% rule implies.

shortAnswer.heading: What does a $700,000 mortgage cost per month?
shortAnswer.html: A $700,000 mortgage costs about $4,424.48 a month in principal and interest at 6.5% on a 30-year fixed term, or $6,097.75 on a 15-year. Depending on your rate (5.0%–7.5%), the 30-year payment runs $3,757.75–$4,894.50. Total 30-year interest at 6.5%: $892,813.

sections.title: $700,000 mortgage payment by rate and term.
sections.note: Principal and interest only — add property taxes, homeowners insurance, and PMI (if under 20% down) for the full monthly cost.

sections.title: What $700,000 of mortgage debt really costs.
paragraphs: At today's representative 6.5% rate, $700,000 of mortgage debt runs $4,424.48 a month on a 30-year term, or $6,097.75 on a 15-year. Over the full term that's $892,813 of interest versus $397,595 — a $495,218 difference for the faster payoff.

Rates move the payment more than most buyers expect: on $700,000, going from 6.0% to 7.0% adds $460.27 a month on a 30-year term — $165,697 over the life of the loan. Across the 5.0%–7.5% range in the table above, the 30-year payment spans $3,757.75 to $4,894.50.

sections.title: Total interest on $700,000 over the full term.
sections.note: At 6.5% on a 30-year term you repay $1,592,813 in total — 2.28× the amount borrowed.

sections.title: First-year amortization: where each payment actually goes.
sections.note: In year one you pay $45,270 of interest but only $7,824 of principal — early payments are mostly interest, which is why extra principal payments early on save so much.

sections.title: PMI, income needed, and the rest of the bill.
paragraphs: Remember that these are principal-and-interest numbers only. Put down less than 20% and PMI adds roughly $292–$583 monthly (0.5–1% of $700,000 per year) until you reach 20% equity. Property tax and insurance frequently add several hundred dollars more — a $700,000 loan with 20% down implies a purchase price near $875,000.

How much income does it take? The common 28% front-end rule says housing costs shouldn't exceed 28% of gross income. On the $4,424.48 payment at 6.5%/30-year, that implies roughly $189,621 of annual income — and more once taxes, insurance, and any PMI join the payment.

sections.title: Nearby loan amounts at 6.5%.
sections.note: Income column applies the 28% front-end rule to the 30-year P&I payment only; taxes and insurance push the real requirement higher.

faq.q: What is the monthly payment on a $700,000 mortgage?
faq.a: At 6.5% on a 30-year fixed, a $700,000 mortgage costs $4,424.48 a month in principal and interest. Across rates from 5.0% to 7.5%, the 30-year payment ranges from $3,757.75 to $4,894.50. Property taxes, insurance, and PMI come on top.

faq.q: How much income do I need for a $700,000 mortgage?
faq.a: Using the 28% front-end rule on the $4,424.48 payment (6.5%, 30-year), you'd want roughly $189,621 of gross annual income for the principal and interest alone. Since lenders count taxes, insurance, PMI, and your other debts too, a comfortable qualifying income is typically higher.

faq.q: How much interest will I pay on a $700,000 mortgage?
faq.a: At 6.5%, total interest comes to $892,813 over a 30-year term versus $397,595 over 15 years — the shorter term saves $495,218. In the first year alone the 30-year loan accrues $45,270 of interest against just $7,824 of principal reduction.

faq.q: Is a 15-year or 30-year term better for a $700,000 loan?
faq.a: The 30-year payment ($4,424.48 at 6.5%) is $1,673.27 cheaper per month than the 15-year ($6,097.75), but costs $495,218 more in lifetime interest. Choose 15 years if the payment fits comfortably; otherwise take the 30-year and make extra principal payments when you can.

faq.q: Does the $700,000 payment include taxes and insurance?
faq.a: No — every figure on this page is principal and interest only. Budget extra for property tax and homeowners insurance (often several hundred dollars monthly, varying by state), plus PMI of roughly $292–$583/month if your down payment is under 20%. With 20% down, $700,000 of financing corresponds to about a $875,000 purchase price.

methodology: Payments use the standard amortization formula M = P·r(1+r)ⁿ / ((1+r)ⁿ − 1) with monthly compounding, on a $700,000 principal. Rates shown (5.0%–7.5%) are illustrative steps, not quotes — your rate depends on credit, points, and the market.
The amortization table applies 6.5%/30-year, computing interest on the running balance each month and rounding to cents, the way a servicer statement does.
All figures are principal and interest only. Property tax, homeowners insurance, HOA dues, and PMI are excluded except where explicitly estimated (PMI shown at 0.5–1% of the loan per year).
Income-needed figures apply the 28% front-end ratio to P&I only. Educational estimates — not lending, tax, or financial advice.
